narrative:
The model estimated your chance of failing the final year at 10%. That means it sees a low but non-zero risk: most similar students would pass, but a small number would not. Under the school’s remedial rule, that risk signal is enough to require additional courses, so treat it as a precaution rather than a certainty.

The strongest factor in the estimate was your record of past class failures: you have none, and this pushed the assessment strongly toward passing. Second was the extra educational support you receive; this also counted as protective. Third was your wish to continue to higher education; every passing student in the comparison group shares that goal, and it too pushed toward passing. These three were the most influential factors, and all point in your favour, which is why the overall fail probability is low. The remaining concern is attendance: you have 10 absences, compared with an average of about 3.8 among students who passed. That weaker signal, along with limited family educational support and no home internet, is what keeps a small risk visible.

To improve your position, make attendance your first priority and aim to bring absences close to the passing average. Keep using the extra support, set a steadier weekly study routine—your current 2–5 hours is typical but could be increased—and ask your mother, teachers, and school staff for structured help with assignments and revision.
